trigger: An airframer launches a new narrowbody (NGSA or fps) and runs an engine competition
response: Bid only for sole source, against a board-set hurdle at least as high as the GTF's (about 10% all-in against an 8% cost of capital; the 10% is an inference from 'more close to double-digit'), with about half the development partnered out. Without a business case, match the airframer's non-commitment and fund only enabling technology. Defend the A320neo franchise early: 'if you miss a cycle ... you get shut out ... for decades'.
lag: Tied to the airframer's decision: on the NMA, P&W's engine decision slipped from about mid-2018 to not before early 2019 while it waited for Boeing, and the NMA never launched
war_game_translation: Launch gtf_next on standard terms, with year = the turn's last (2028 in turn 1), in the turn an airframer discloses NGSA or fps on pw_gtf2; disclose the commitment. Engine, run calib turn 1, airframes in 2028: NGSA on pw_gtf2 +0.96 (+1.98 with gtf_upgrade in 2026); NGSA falls back to CFM -3.11 (-1.74); fps on ours +1.65; both +3.35. NGSA-only hedge without a disclosure (inference): break-even p = cost/(cost+gain) = 1.20/(1.20+3.72), about 1 in 4, with the upgrade in 2026; 0.86/(0.86+0.96+3.11), about 1 in 6, without the upgrade overlap. Launch when p is at least about 0.45 (0.38 without the overlap), which adds the $1B doctrine allowance. p = P(launch this turn, about 0.7 from the airframers' whatif timing payoffs) x P(names pw_gtf2, about 0.3 with RR in play, 0.7 without), so about 0.2 on turn 1 with RR: no hedge. fps (break-even about 2 in 5) gets no hedge.

trigger: An airframer launches a widebody Re-engine (787 Re-engine or A350 Re-engine)
response: Abstain. P&W calls itself 'narrow-body focused' and took widebody risk only in a 50/50 Joint Venture with GE (the GP7000, now out of production). It passed on the 787, which UTC's CEO later called under-investment rather than doctrine. Its 2019 widebody plan appears in no later source (inference: never executed).
war_game_translation: Do Nothing on pw_wb; the flip is inactive at calibration. Engine, turn 1: pw_wb is -3.65 even with the 787 Re-engine on pw_wb_new and -4.10 on the A350 Re-engine (best options case -3.56 with the upgrade). Flip only if a Re-engine is disclosed on pw_wb_new, airframer_incentive_b > 0, whatif is at least +$1.5B after strain and no narrowbody programme is in development (gtf_upgrade counts).

trigger: An airframer or airline selects a rival engine
response: Let it go rather than match price ('we were disciplined ... we don't regret it'), accept 40-50% of a shared platform, and win back on product. P&W claimed 56% of A320neo selections from June 2017 to June 2018, against LEAP's almost 10:1 lead in 2017 order intake reported by a 2019 industry brief (the two are not reconciled). An analyst reported Airbus shifting allocation toward CFM in 2020.
war_game_translation: Do not switch to aggressive terms to chase. Cancel gtf_next if no airframe flies it. Fund gtf_upgrade: NGSA on CFM is -1.74 with it and -3.11 without (engine, turn 1).

trigger: An airframer asks for price concessions or compensation
response: No deep discounts past launch mode. Share technology-driven cost-outs with airframers, not pure margin. Pay when at fault (the $196M 2017 diversion charge). Buy platform positions with exclusivity payments tied to future sales or flight hours. UTC group, not P&W engines (parent doctrine applied by analogy, inference): Collins/UTAS traded cost-downs for volume guarantees under Boeing's PFS 2.0, and UTC walked away from a Boeing price-down on a non-engine product with no aftermarket.
war_game_translation: Stay on standard terms. Aggressive terms raise Airbus's NGSA incentive from +1.75 to +6.73 but cut our NGSA win to -3.66, below losing it (-3.11); fps aggressive -1.75 against -0.64 on CFM (engine, turn 1). Flip only if whatif(aggressive, selected) beats whatif(standard, not selected).

response: Take the platform when a rival's programme fails: Dassault moved the Falcon 6X to P&W's PW812 after Safran's Silvercrest problems. In October 2020 P&W said it would keep gaining A320neo share, having risen from 43% to about 55% over the prior 1.5 years, mostly before COVID; the premise that rivals were weakened came from an analyst's question, which management did not dispute.
lag: 1-2 years (inference: Silvercrest problems to the February 2018 Falcon 6X selection)
war_game_translation: After rr_durability_crisis or ultrafan_test_setback, disclose a gtf_next offer on standard terms to the airframer waiting on UltraFan; launch it if that airframer signals pw_gtf2. Do not join the Joint Venture that turn.

trigger: A rival engine maker wins big or out-innovates
response: Answer with incremental product, never price: fix durability, then the GTF Advantage. Prefer an upgrade of the incumbent to a clean sheet, as with the F135 core upgrade. Reuse the GTF core to displace rivals where possible: the PW800 replaced Rolls-Royce on the Gulfstream G500/G600, a competitive win rather than a response to a stumble.
war_game_translation: Commit gtf_upgrade if not done; keep standard terms; no panic launch of gtf_next without an airframer signal.

trigger: Our own durability crisis (GTF early issues 2016-18; the 2023 powder-metal recall)
response: Divert production engines to spares and take a one-off charge; compensate airlines bilaterally within the provision ($5.4bn gross, $2.9bn net, about 80% compensation); push 49% to partners; expand MRO; fix forward with block upgrades and the GTF Advantage, then charge for the Hot Section Plus kit. P&W claimed about 40% share in February 2024 and aimed to hold it (view).
lag: Weeks to divert; about a quarter for the charge; 2-3 years for the upgrade
war_game_translation: Under gtf_durability_crisis, commit gtf_upgrade that turn if not already committed (+1.76 alone in turn 1); keep standard terms; no pw_wb; keep a committed gtf_next (do not cancel).

response: Cut E&D (about $300M at P&W) and capex (about $500M); RTX cut about 20% of commercial-aero headcount, about 15,000 positions across Collins and P&W. Suspend buybacks for 2020, partly out of sensitivity to struggling customers, and hold the dividend. Keep the rate-63 capacity plan and suppliers warm through COVID. Use idle shops to retrofit the GTF fleet.
war_game_translation: Under nb_demand_shock, keep a committed gtf_next and the upgrade; defer an uncommitted gtf_next one turn unless an airframer has disclosed a launch on pw_gtf2.

trigger: An airframer's quality or rate problems (e.g. 737 MAX grounding, Airbus rate ambitions)
response: Plan on the airframer's own revised numbers (the 737 MAX halt and half-rate restart, 2020); add no capacity to exploit a grounding (2-2.5 years to add forging); haircut airframer rate ambitions to 63-65; keep building and buying through a Boeing strike to keep the supply base warm. UTC group, not P&W engines (by analogy, inference): impairment tests on Collins 737 MAX content treated the grounding as temporary. Strength rests on the P&W capacity items (P-0079, P-0069, P-2047).
war_game_translation: No order under boeing_quality_escape or certification_scrutiny. An fps slip delays our engine's value with the airframe; weight NGSA over fps when choosing which disclosure to answer.

trigger: Technology slip on our own engine
response: Slip quietly, add testing, do not cancel: GTF Advantage entry into service went from 2024 to '25-ish' to certification in 2025. Carry launch customers' slips (CSeries, MRJ).
lag: About 1 year per slip (GTF Advantage: 2024 plan, 2025 certification)
war_game_translation: Under gtf_next_test_setback or engine_maturity_slip, keep a committed gtf_next (each extra year costs 10% of capex; cancelling is barred while an airframe flies it); never add pw_wb on top.

response: Second-source, embed staff at suppliers, insource critical parts (the $285M Asheville foundry). In 2022 P&W worked through a castings supplier's shortfall rather than switching, missing about 70 Airbus engines in Q1. In the powder-metal crisis it kept Airbus OE engines flowing first, and in 2025 said the OE/spares mix had not shifted; rationing beyond that is inference. Boeing's CEO says P&W and CFM compete for the same castings.
war_game_translation: Under supply_chain_crunch (strain +50%): the engine charges strain on any two overlapping P&W development windows, including the upgrade's 3-year window and the Joint Venture, although the rules text names only narrowbody-plus-widebody overlaps. With gtf_upgrade started in 2026, launch a turn-1 gtf_next only into a disclosure; otherwise move it to turn 2 (2029 or later).

trigger: A partner proposes a Joint Venture (Rolls-Royce UltraFan narrowbody, jv_pw)
response: Share risk and investment, never core technology ('you spread risk, you spread investment through JVs, but you don't share technologies'); joining RR's UltraFan would share RR's technology, not P&W's (inference). Lead every collaboration except the 50/50 Engine Alliance with GE; co-owned IAE with RR until 2012. The 2012 P&W-RR midsize JV left no trace after July 2012 (inference). When the partner had no business case for the A320neo, P&W went alone.
war_game_translation: join_rr_jv is free unless RR launches uf_nb as jv_pw in the same turn, and irreversible once it does: validate rejects cancel uf_nb from P&W, so only RR controls the exit. Set it when P(an airframer selects UltraFan this turn | RR launches jv_pw) is at least about 0.23 (break-even 3.71/(3.71+16.64), about 0.18, plus the $1B doctrine allowance) and no gtf_next is aimed at the same airframer unless whatif favours the pair. Engine, turn 1, with the upgrade: joined with NGSA on UltraFan +14.91, nobody selects -1.95, NGSA on CFM -5.45, RR cancels in turn 2 +0.87; staying out -1.74 or +1.76. Without the upgrade: NGSA on UltraFan +13.71, fps on UltraFan +11.02, no selection -3.54. RR earns +23.90 solo against +11.79 in the Joint Venture when selected, so a jv_pw offer signals RR rates its own selection odds below about 23%. Turn 1: default off; disclose conditional willingness to join in any turn for which an airframer discloses UltraFan.

trigger: An airframer cancels or pauses a programme flying our engine
response: Stand by the customer through delays, formalise a pause by contract, and run a finished engine as an aftermarket business.
war_game_translation: Cancel gtf_next (or pw_wb) in the turn its only airframe is cancelled, if no other live airframe flies it.

trigger: An airframer pushes into the engine aftermarket
response: Threaten to reprice OE if airframers take more of the aftermarket; defend with proprietary parts, nacelle bundling and fleet-management plans.
war_game_translation: No direct lever; stay on standard terms and keep fleet economics in the upgrade.

trigger: CFM/GE commits its advanced ducted narrowbody engine (cfm_ducted), or offers it on aggressive terms (five-player game)
response: Let a rival's price win go rather than match it ('we were disciplined ... we don't regret it'), accept 40-50% of a shared platform, and win back on product. No deep discounts past launch mode; competitors that offer big discounts and guarantees are a known risk in our filings. LEAP took 54% of A320neo orders against the GTF's 46% by 2016.
war_game_translation: Snapshot, run pw-5p-scratch, round 1, upgrade in 2026: stay on standard terms and launch gtf_next only into a disclosure. CFM/GE's ducted commitment raises Airbus's fallback from the LEAP derivative (+41.48, NGSA 2028) to +46.55, cutting our edge (ours +48.29) from +6.81 to +1.74. On aggressive terms CFM/GE's engine pays Airbus +52.69, above ours; matching with aggressive terms gives Airbus +53.09 but leaves us at -2.14, below losing NGSA (-1.74): do not match. Airbus now names us over UltraFan only if it rates our launch 2.25 times as likely as RR's (1.32 times against the derivative), so halve the round-1 naming odds behind the NGSA hedge (inference).

trigger: CFM/GE orders its LEAP durability upgrade (leap_upgrade: 5pp of A320neo deliveries from P&W)
response: Answer with incremental durability product, not price: Block D, the GTF Advantage and the Hot Section Plus kit, charged for case by case. LEAP's almost 10:1 order lead in 2017 followed doubts about GTF durability, which cost campaigns we chose not to buy on price; 'time on wing ... is the name of the game'.
war_game_translation: Snapshot, run pw-5p-scratch: commit gtf_upgrade if it is not booked. Its value is +1.76 (round 1) whether or not CFM/GE upgrades; CFM/GE's upgrade alone costs us 0.67 (0.28 if NGSA enters service in 2035) and cuts our A320neo engines from 960 to 840 a year, missing gtf_base; with both upgrades we hold 960 (+1.09). A round-2 gtf_upgrade (books 2031) is still worth +1.15 and still meets credibility. No terms response.

trigger: CFM/GE commits the RISE open fan (cfm_open_fan, entry into service from 2045) or lobbies governments on emissions
response: Treat the open fan as 'a long time from now' and answer inside the geared architecture: composite fan, CMC hot section, new gear. A 2019 industry brief reported a planned next-generation GTF aimed at CFM's open rotor; we prefer enhanced packages to clean sheets.
war_game_translation: Snapshot, run pw-5p-scratch: no order, and never pull gtf_next forward. The open fan needs 9 development years, so CFM/GE must launch it by 2036 for 2045. In no NGSA launch year we ran is it Airbus's best engine (NGSA 2036: +15.47, +18.87 with aggressive terms and lobbying, against +22.20 on ours and +21.44 on the ducted engine). NGSA on the open fan leaves us 1,080 engines a year to 2044 and none after (+0.48); lobbying alone changes nothing for us. If an airframer discloses the open fan, disclose a gtf_next offer ready at its entry into service (row 5).

trigger: CFM/GE partners with Embraer (embraer_partner) or upgrades the GEnx (genx_upgrade)
response: No precedent in our evidence. Embraer's GTF aircraft was in our 2017 certification plan, and we stand by regional customers through delays (MRJ, CSeries, SpaceJet).
war_game_translation: Snapshot, run pw-5p-scratch: no lever and no order. Neither move changes our payoff (+1.76 with the upgrade); Boeing's fps Joint Venture with Embraer on pw_gtf2 still pays us +3.32 (fps 2028, gtf_next 2029).

trigger: An airframer launches a new narrowbody while CFM/GE has committed no new engine (the LEAP derivative, cfm_leap_plus, is the fallback)
response: Defend the A320neo franchise early ('if you miss a cycle ... you get shut out ... for decades'); bid where we have a clear technology lead; sole source only, and match the airframer's commitment.
war_game_translation: Snapshot, run pw-5p-scratch: disclose a sole-source, standard-terms gtf_next ready at the airframe's entry into service (launch in the airframe's launch year + 1, not before 2029 after a 2026 upgrade). Against the derivative ours adds +6.81 for Airbus (NGSA 2028: +48.29 against +41.48) and +3.35 for Boeing (fps 2028: +15.93 against +12.58); naming pw_gtf2 costs an airframer nothing, since it falls back down the same CFM chain (inference). Launch on the profile §6 tests: NGSA 2028 with gtf_next 2029 pays +2.30 against -1.74 lost; a hedge cancelled in 2031 costs 1.53, break-even about 0.27, flip at 0.45.
